Pacific jack mackerel, Trachurus symmetricus, exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of a moderately fast-growing pelagic carangid, with reproductive output tightly linked to thermal conditions. Females attain sexual maturation and begin spawning once they reach a total length of approximately 31 cm [Lp = approximately 31 cm], a size that indicates the onset of puberty and the transition to the reproductively active adult phase. Under thermal regimes characteristic of its upwelling-influenced habitat, at a water temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], the maximum instantaneous reproductive rate, expressed as the product of spawning frequency and batch fecundity, equates to roughly 53,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 53,000 eggs per spawning event] with one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year]. This high daily output underpins a considerable lifetime fecundity, allowing the species to exploit pulsed productivity events. The comparatively modest size at puberty reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early investment in reproduction, a common pattern among small to medium-sized carangids inhabiting productive eastern boundary current ecosystems.

The early life stages of Pacific jack mackerel are characterized by rapid development and a small initial body size. At a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the period from fertilization through eclosion and the subsequent brief lecithotrophic phase is completed in approximately 1.4 days [ab = approximately 1.4 days]. At the moment of chorion rupture and emergence of the yolk-sac larva, the wet weight of the newly hatched individual is remarkably low, recorded at 0.000278 grams [Wwb = 0.000278 grams]. This minute mass, typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts with small, transparent eggs, necessitates an immediate transition to exogenous feeding upon yolk depletion. The combination of a warm incubation temperature and a short egg stage facilitates a rapid entry into the planktonic larval phase, a critical period where growth and survival are strongly dependent on the availability of suitable microzooplankton prey and the avoidance of a wide array of pelagic predators.

As individuals grow and transition from the planktonic larval phase through metamorphosis to the juvenile stage, their weight increases substantially. Upon reaching the size at first reproduction at 31 cm total length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at roughly 254 grams [Wwp = roughly 254 grams]. This value represents a massive increase from the initial larval mass and reflects the accumulation of somatic and gonadal tissues necessary for successful spawning. Continued growth into the adult phase leads to an ultimate asymptotic mass of approximately 4355 grams [Wwi = approximately 4355 grams], a size that is typically attained by the largest, oldest individuals in the population. The relationship between length and weight reveals a strongly positive allometric growth pattern, where depth and girth increase disproportionately relative to length, allowing the fish to carry substantial lipid reserves and a large body of developing oocytes during the spawning season.

The ultimate total length that a Pacific jack mackerel can achieve under natural conditions has been documented at 81 centimeters [Li = 81 centimeters], a size that represents the upper boundary of the species' morphological potential. This maximum recorded length is associated with the oldest fish in the population, which can achieve a remarkable lifespan. Under the cool, productive conditions of the California Current at 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], the maximum documented longevity for this species approaches an impressive thirty years [am = thirty years], a remarkably long lifespan for a pelagic teleost of this body size. This extended duration of life, when coupled with the high daily egg production rate, results in an extraordinary lifetime reproductive output. Such a strategy argues for a bet-hedging approach to recruitment, where adult fish survive across multiple years of varying environmental quality, ensuring that at least some cohorts encounter favorable conditions for larval survival and subsequent juvenile recruitment into the adult stock.

When comparing the life-history strategy of Trachurus symmetricus to other members of the Carangidae, its moderate growth rate and prolonged reproductive window become apparent. The species does not exhibit the extremely accelerated life cycle of some tropical carangids; instead, its thirty-year lifespan (thirty years) [am = thirty years] places it as a relatively long-lived, iteroparous spawner within the genus at a temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C]. This longevity is facilitated by the cool, 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C] environment of its core habitat, which slows metabolic aging and allows for the remarkable ultimate weight of 4355 grams [Wwi = 4355 grams] to be achieved over many years. A striking feature is the contrast between the tiny initial mass of 0.000278 grams [Wwb = 0.000278 grams] and the massive adult body size, representing a weight increase of over fifteen million-fold from the yolk-sac larva to the fully grown adult. This immense growth potential, combined with a long reproductive life, underscores the species' ecological success as a dominant mid-level predator in the California Current ecosystem.
